20443-the-letter-of-the-contract:
Basil King, the Canadian novelist, wrote The Letter of the Contract as a novel of home life and hard choices. Its heroine looks back on one small act that changed everything. Had she looked in on the children after her coffee, as she generally did, her whole life might have been different.

Instead she went down to the drawing room to write a note. From that tiny turn, the story builds its account of marriage, duty, and the terms people bind themselves by. King asks what we owe to the letter of our promises, and what we owe beyond it.
20787-punctuation-a-primer-of-informatio:
A man in a white hat and polished boots shows, without marks, how wild a sentence can run. Punctuation, a primer on the marks of punctuation, uses such tricks to teach its point. Commas, stops, and colons here get their due at last.

Frederick W. Hamilton wrote short primers that made dry craft clear and fun. This one sorts the marks by use, with crisp rules and bright cases. Writers, printers, and students all stood to gain from its order. The book proves a small point well made: clear marks save clear thought, on every page they touch.
21049-the-curlytops-and-their-pets-or-un:
Janet Martin loads her toy ship with oranges, gold, diamonds, and chocolate cake at the brook. Howard R. Garis opens The Curlytops and Their Pets on that rich, childish cargo. Teddy, her brother, sails boats beside her behind the house.

Ted and Janet, the Curlytops, collect pets and scrapes in this set of tales. Uncle Toby's strange collection of creatures gives this volume its hook. Garis, who created Uncle Wiggily, wrote shelves of warm animal tales for children. His Curlytops show the same gift: small wonders, kind hearts, and pets with minds of their own.
21537-expansion-and-conflict:
William E. Dodd, professor of American history at Chicago, wrote Expansion and Conflict, copyrighted in 1915. The book opens with Andrew Jackson defying the coalition that made John Quincy Adams president. Let the people rule, Jackson answered, as the party of the West rose.

Chapters move through Jackson's triumph, distress and reaction, and the militant South. War and conquest, the abolitionists, and a burst of prosperity follow. Stephen A. Douglas and Abraham Lincoln anchor the last third of the book. The appeal to arms and the collapse of the Confederacy close a swift survey of a nation splitting apart.
21643-the-kensington-district:
G. E. Mitton writes, and Sir Walter Besant edits, The Kensington District in the Fascination of London series. The booklet appeared in 1903, at one shilling and sixpence in cloth. Holland House, drawn by Herbert Railton, fronts the volume.

Besant's great survey aimed to record the whole of London, street by street. Kensington's palaces, gardens, and famed residents fill this part. The series also covered the Strand, Westminster, Chelsea, and Hampstead. Local folk and students of London both formed its target readers. Much of the city's interest, the editors held, lies in these street associations, and Kensington proves the point.
21785-poems-of-rural-life-in-the-dorset-:
Dorset farm life speaks in its own tongue in these poems by William Barnes, gathered here in one volume in 1903. Barnes wrote in the dialect of his home county, with its soft spellings and old words. A guide to the words and their sounds waits at the back of the book. His preface, written in June 1879, calls the poems glimpses of life and landscape in Dorset.

The verses move with the farming year: spring woods, Easter, milkmaids, great oak trees, and evening twilight. Barnes knew this world from inside and loved it without fuss. Thomas Hardy admired him, and later readers have too. The poems keep a whole way of rural English speech alive on the page.
22050-life-and-conduct:
J. Cameron Lees, a minister of the Church of Scotland, gathered his counsel in Life and Conduct, issued in 1896 for the Guild series. The book speaks chiefly to young men starting out. Lees lists the works he consulted and owns his debts openly. His aim is a plain guide to character that a busy reader can use.

Chapters treat habits, work, friendship, reading, and the formation of a steady mind. Lees mixes moral advice with literary illustration. The tone is earnest and Presbyterian, without gloom. Such conduct books filled the shelves of self-improving homes. Lees's volume is a fair, kindly example of the breed.

govdocs-archive_org-NrcReportOnPossibleL: A report of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission examines the possible long-term health effects of short-term exposure to radiation. Federal science reports of this kind weigh animal studies, accident data, and dose records to judge what a brief exposure may do over a lifetime. govdocs-archive_org-cksonKingsDethroned1:
Kings Dethroned, published in 1922, was a sweeping attack on the authorities of modern science, and this extract holds its chapter 'Relativity Debunked.' The chapter takes on Albert Einstein's theory of relativity, then newly famous and still fighting for acceptance.

It covers the theory's reception at the Royal Astronomical Society in 1919, when eclipse observation results were announced as proof of Einstein. The author treats that moment as a coronation to undo, arguing the evidence had been oversold. The extract is early anti-relativity literature, held without endorsement as a record of the resistance Einstein faced.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-OtmoorProductio: A contents page survives from a manuscript about the investigation of James Earl Ray. Among its listed parts are a New Orleans trip and the Provincial Motel, a stop in Ray's travels that investigators retraced. The author is not identified. govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
In May 2016, a federal court in Buenos Aires found eighteen Argentine military officers guilty for their part in Operation Condor, the cross-border system of repression run by South America's military regimes. The National Security Archive's electronic briefing book, edited by Carlos Osorio and Peter Kornbluh, marked the verdict the day it landed.

Condor let member regimes seize, torture, and kill each other's dissidents far from home, and victims came from several countries. A trial that treated that system itself as the crime was a first in the region. The Archive hailed the ruling as a major milestone. Readers get both the outcome and the context: how a secret pact among dictatorships ended, forty years on, in open court.
lessons-in-music-form-a-manual-of-analys:
Percy Goetschius wrote Lessons in Music Form as a manual of analysis. Its subtitle promises all the structural factors used in musical composition. Oliver Ditson published it in Boston for a dollar and a half.

Goetschius held a royal professorship in Württemberg. He had written many theory books before this one. Here he teaches how pieces are built, section by section. Students learn to hear phrases, periods, and larger designs. The manual suits composers, teachers, and serious listeners alike. Examples from real composers anchor each design he names. Goetschius insists form is heard, not merely diagrammed.
miss-civilization-a-comedy-in-one-act:
Richard Harding Davis wrote this one-act comedy, first printed in Collier's Weekly. He founded it on a story by James Harvey Smith. The scene is a dining room on Long Island at Christmas. Silver presents still sit in red flannel bags on the sideboard.

The house belongs to railroad president James K. Gardner. His daughter Alice faces three uninvited guests. Their aliases are Gentleman Joe, Reddy the Kid, and Grand Stand Harry. A police captain completes the cast. Davis builds a light comedy of burglary and manners, where the young lady proves more than a match for her visitors.
nasa-tm-19670008871-excitation-of-hydrog:
S. P. Khare, working at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland as a resident research associate, studies a basic atomic collision in this paper. It is the third part of his series on exciting the hydrogen molecule by electron impact. This part treats singlet-triplet excitations, collisions in which an incoming electron flips the molecule into a spin state that light alone cannot reach.

Khare used one-center wave functions developed by Huzinaga, together with the Ochkur approximation, to compute the exchange excitation. Because the lowest triplet state pushes the molecule's two atoms apart, these excitations split hydrogen molecules into separate atoms. The shape of his predicted curve for that splitting matched the lab data of Corrigan in general. He also computed rates for the splitting and for related continuous radiation, and compared them with the measurements at hand.
nasa-tm-19690018501-possible-initial-evi:
F. W. Stecker, of the Theoretical Studies Branch at Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this preprint, X-641-69-232. He presented it at an astronomy symposium in Rome in May 1969. Stecker compares recent cosmic background gamma ray observations against spectra predicted by several cosmic interactions. He argues the best match points beyond our own galaxy.

The even, all-sky gamma glow is best explained, he finds, by decaying particles born in extragalactic cosmic ray collisions. That reading implies such sources were more active in the distant past. They began forming only tens of millions of years after the big bang, on his estimate. Today's extragalactic cosmic ray flow is inferred as a tiny fraction of the galactic one.
nasa-tm-19690021377-primary-chemical-met:
Aaron Fisher, John Grimsley, Thomas Sciacca, and Charles Staugaitis, of Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this June 1969 report, X-735-69-230. They catalog the primary techniques for evaluating magnetic tapes: chemical, metallurgical, and electro-optical. Tapes then recorded much of NASA's spacecraft and test data, so judging tape quality before use protected whole archives.

The chemical section runs from light spectrum tests to heat-based breakdown tools and thermal analyzers. Each tool reads a different trait of the tape's binder and oxide coating. Metal and machine procedures follow: cross-section making, close-up views, and head-tape fit checks. Blocking, tensile, hardness, and surface roughness tests complete the practical kit the authors assembled.
nasa-tm-19700021514-description-and-perf:
Pierre A. Thollot, Richard C. Bainbridge, and James Nestor of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 energy conversion conference in Las Vegas. It describes the electrical subsystem of a Brayton power system. The system size ranges from two to fifteen kilowatts of electric power.

The subsystem covers the alternator and the gear that conditions its output. Liquid coolant runs through a heat exchanger and the alternator housing to carry heat away. The paper gives both the design and how the hardware performed in tests. Power systems of this class were leading candidates for long missions in deep space.
nasa-tm-19700025308-a-preliminary-analys:
Clarke T. Hackler of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this internal note, number 66-M-32. It gives a first analysis of failure detection during the lunar module's powered descent. It also covers how the guidance system would be watched for faults during that flight phase, the most demanding minutes of the mission.

During descent the guidance flies the craft almost the whole way down, while the crew only monitors. Hackler notes that comparing the primary and abort guidance paths builds confidence that both work. Spotting that one has failed, though, is easier than proving which one failed. His study takes up that gap: watching both systems, detecting a failure, and isolating it while a safe abort is still possible.
nasa-tm-19710011034-a-summary-of-major-n:
Kennedy Space Center issued this reference as Historical Report Number 1, revised in 1970. It sums up major NASA launchings from October 1, 1958 through September 30, 1970. Those dates span the agency's first twelve years. The summary covers flights from the Eastern Test Range and the Western Test Range.

The Historical and Library Services Section at Kennedy compiled the record. Readers get a compact account of the launch campaigns that built the early space program. It captures the shift from small test rockets to crewed Apollo flights. Historians still use such summaries to check dates, vehicles, and launch sites.
nasa-tm-19710011291-experimental-investi:
James E Calogeras, Charles M Mehalic, and Paul L Burstadt of the Lewis Research Center ran this turbojet distortion study. Screens placed before a J85 engine warped the incoming air pressure on purpose. The team measured how each warp pattern cut the engine stall margin, the safety gap before the compressor stalls.

One clear result stood out. The compressor had a critical distortion angle of sixty degrees. Stall losses for single and multiple patterns tracked a simple index based on the lowest mean pressure in any sixty degree sector. Hub radial distortion changed pumping and pressure but not stall margin. Tip radial distortion did change stall margin.
nasa-tm-19710011753-a-study-of-the-requi:
R W Jech of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for an April 1971 meeting on composite materials in Anaheim. It asks how long reinforcing fibers must be inside a composite to do their job. The test material paired tungsten wire fibers with a copper matrix. Length relative to width is called the aspect ratio.

Jech compared pull out specimens in tension and in stress rupture tests. The critical aspect ratio in hot stress rupture tests ran slightly above the tension value. Above that ratio, the tungsten fiber controlled how long specimens lasted. Below it, the copper matrix controlled failure time. The results guide fiber length choices for parts under long hot loads.
nasa-tm-19720013138-the-recurrent-nature:
A NASA preprint on solar radio noise studies type 1 noise active regions from 1965 through 1969. Its author was a NASA associate with the University of Maryland. Type 1 noise comes from active regions on the Sun at meter wavelengths. Because the Sun rotates, a long-lived region returns to view roughly every twenty-seven days.

The study tracks that recurrence across five years of observations. The abstract reports a repeat period slightly longer than twenty-seven days for these noise sources. It also finds that the number of recurrent trends for a source is generally four. Discussion connects the noise sources closely with the active regions where proton flares occur. Earlier work by Sakurai and Stone on the 1968 season had found the same near twenty-seven-day rhythm.
nasa-tm-19720022222-predictions-of-vehic:
A NASA radiation forecast predicts the electron and proton fluxes the UK-4 spacecraft would meet in orbit. UK-4 was a British satellite built with NASA cooperation, and the scan garbles the forecast's author names. Designers needed to know how much particle radiation UK-4 would meet in orbit. Its planned path crossed Earth's radiation belts twice on every revolution.

To make the predictions, the authors added up proton and electron flows along the planned flight path. Current models of Earth's field and of the radiation environment fed those sums. Because the launch was set for late 1971, close after a solar maximum, the electron data needed two adjustments. Artificial electrons left by the 1962 Starfish explosion had to be decayed away to natural background levels. Lasting solar-cycle effects in the outer belt, missing from the older environment model, also had to be folded in.
one-day-more-a-play-in-one-act:
Joseph Conrad wrote this one-act play for the stage. The Beaumont Press issued it as its sixth book. Only 274 numbered copies were printed in this edition. Captain Hagberd is a retired coasting skipper in the cast. His son Harry ran away from home as a boy.

Josiah Carvil is a blind, widowed former shipbuilder. His daughter Bessie, about twenty-five, guides him patiently. The scene is a small sea port at dusk. Two yellow brick cottages stand by a lamp post. Carvil scolds Bessie for hurrying his steps homeward. Conrad builds quiet tension from waiting and return.

the-sculpture-and-mural-decorations-of-t: Stella Perry's pictorial survey records the art of the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition in San Francisco — the sculptures and murals that adorned its palaces and courts. the-wonders-of-instinct-chapters-in-the-: Fabre's Wonders of Instinct explores the amazing life of insects. The devoted student of nature watches wasps, bees, and beetles with loving patience. Long and careful watching reveals marvel after marvel. Nature writing at its very finest.
un-un-res-united-nations-participation-a:
American membership in the new United Nations was put into law by the United Nations Participation Act of 1945. Congress passed it months after the UN Charter was signed in San Francisco. The act gave the president the legal tools to seat the United States inside the world body from its first days.

The text covers the American ambassador's post, payment of dues, and the president's powers on the Security Council. It also sets limits on when American forces can serve under UN command. The act still stands, much amended, as the base law of the American role at the UN.
